drafts.title: Colorado heat pump credit: $333 off the invoice
drafts.body:
Pricing a heat pump in Colorado? The state credit is $1,000 for an air-source unit installed in 2026.

And your contractor has to take at least $333 of it right off your invoice.

Ask for it by name when you get quotes. Don't leave it on the table.

drafts.title: $30 part that keeps a lineman alive: the generator mistake (Wed 8-9 AM)
drafts.angle: Plain winter outage safety for older homeowners, riding the Hurricane Lana trend. One soft line on why he likes batteries. No politics, no meme.
bullets: Plugging a generator into a dryer outlet (a "suicide cord") can backfeed the power lines and electrocute utility workers fixing them.
Safe route: an interlock kit (often around $30 for the part) plus a power inlet box, installed by a licensed electrician.
Simplest safe option: extension cords from the generator straight to the fridge and a lamp.
Run generators outside, away from windows; carbon monoxide is the other killer. Have him confirm the interlock price locally before posting.
drafts.body:
$30. That's about what the part costs that keeps your generator from killing a lineman.

Every storm, somebody plugs a generator into the dryer outlet. It works, so they think it's fine. But that power can run backward up the line and hit the guy up the pole trying to get your lights back on.

The fix is an interlock kit and an inlet box. Have an electrician put it in. Or just run extension cords to the fridge.

My plan this winter: [my setup ___ / I went battery because ___].

What's your outage plan? Generator, battery, or candles and hope?
drafts.ocr_why: High save and share value, reply magnet; goes Strong if he adds his own setup or a panel photo. Keep the battery line to one sentence.
drafts.pixel: Optional, at the breaker panel: "If you own a generator, look for this. If you don't have it, call an electrician."
drafts.target: Reply under a big weather or prepper account's Hurricane Lana prep post with the short safety line.
